name: Expiry — the freshness check for anything you wrote about software
one_liner: Paste a URL (your blog post, README, SKILL.md or any tutorial) and Expiry returns a shareable "freshness card": each factual claim about software marked still true / out of date / unverifiable with a live source, a 0-100 Still True score, and a weekly re-check if you save it.
problem: Everyone who writes about software — blog posts, READMEs, agent SKILL.md files, docs pages, course notes — has content quietly going stale: model names, pricing, CLI flags, free-tier limits, "the latest version is...". Readers hit it, agents ingest it, and the author has no idea. Today the only options are re-reading your own post by hand, or asking an agent and hoping it has current knowledge (it usually doesn't — training cutoffs are exactly the problem). The bookmarks show this pain named out loud: skill-diet exists partly because skill files "go stale" and "no longer match the tool", and the whole point of Parallel's new Decisions API is that decision models "lack the recency of current news". Expiry is the consumer-grade version of that: one URL in, one dated verdict card out.
target_customer: Devrel people, indie hackers, technical bloggers, OSS maintainers and agent-skill authors — the crowd on X, r/devrel, r/ExperiencedDevs, Hacker News and the Claude/Cursor skill communities. Free tool; no buyer. If it grows, teams with docs sites would pay for the weekly crawl.
why_now: Parallel's Decisions API launched 27 Oct 2026 (the bookmarked @p0 post): web-grounded TYPED answers — a probability that a statement is true, or a choice/score — at $0.001 per request, up to 100 questions bundled per request, 200ms–1s latency, 5,000 free requests for new accounts plus a recurring $5/month free allowance (docs.parallel.ai/getting-started/pricing). That is the exact missing primitive: before this, "is this sentence still true?" meant building your own search + LLM + citation pipeline per claim and paying per token. Now 100 extracted claims from a blog post = one request = one tenth of a cent, with citations attached. Confirmed: choice and score question types exist, citations come back at the response level, and ToS explicitly permit integrating the API into applications served to end users (per-visitor fresh results, no shared republished cache).
comparables: Nothing found that does URL → per-claim freshness card. Adjacent: (1) agent skills `skill-auditing` (BCGen) and `freshness-auditor` (bootgs) audit a skill file's claims against live docs — but they are SKILL.md files you run inside your own agent, not a link anyone can click, and they produce no shareable artefact; (2) SERP Delta (github.com/researchsite/SerpDelta) is a Streamlit "LLM knowledge gap detector" with a staleness score — zero stars, no hosted instance found; (3) HowToAI Hallucination Checker labels pasted claims right/wrong/out-of-date, but it is paste-text, generic news fact-checking, no URL ingest, no card, no re-check; (4) DocsAlot's docs benchmark (docsalot.slashml.com/benchmarks) ranks 215 docs sites but was last updated June 2026 and is site-level, not claim-level; (5) Shields.io / cardd.cc badges show only a timestamp, never whether the content is still true. The gap: a free, no-signup, one-URL web app whose output is a posted image card with a number on it, plus a weekly re-check.
market_note: No market in the paid sense — free tool. Cost estimate: one check ≈ 1 Decisions request ($0.001) + one small LLM extraction call (~$0.002), so ~$3 per 1,000 checks; a viral day of 10,000 checks costs roughly $30 (estimate). Parallel's free allowance covers launch traffic. If it grew, the paid shape would be a docs-site weekly crawl for devrel teams.
risks: Claim extraction quality is the whole product — if the LLM pulls out vague or non-checkable sentences, the verdicts look dumb and the score is noise. Mitigation: hard filter to claims containing a version, price, number, flag, model name or "latest/current". Second: Parallel's citations come back at the response level, not per answer, so "what's true now" needs a second pass or looser wording — never show a citation as if it proves a specific claim. Third: false "OUT OF DATE" verdicts on someone's post are embarrassing in public; needs an unverifiable bucket used generously and a visible "this is triage, not proof" line.
riskiest_assumptions: 1) An LLM can reliably extract atomic, web-checkable software claims from arbitrary prose — unproven, and everything else depends on it. 2) Parallel's probability on "is this statement still true?" is actually discriminative for version/pricing claims rather than hovering near 0.5 — the docs call it an evidence-grounded estimate, not a calibrated forecast. 3) Authors find a low score funny rather than insulting, and post it.
first_customers: The builder's own X followers on launch day; devrel people (the ones who maintain tutorials and feel this pain monthly); OSS maintainers with long READMEs; the Claude/Cursor skill-authoring crowd the bookmarks point at (nicopreme's skill-diet thread replies are literally people worried about stale skills); r/devrel, r/ExperiencedDevs, Hacker News "Show HN".
validation_test: This week: run Expiry by hand on 10 real posts — 3 of the builder's own, 4 popular dev tutorials from 2023-2024, 3 public SKILL.md files — and manually grade every verdict. Pass: ≥80% of OUT OF DATE verdicts are genuinely out of date and each post surfaces at least 2 real rotted claims. Fail: mostly unverifiable, or false positives above 1 in 5 → the extraction prompt is the problem, not the idea. Then post one card ("my own guide scored 41") and see if replies ask for their own URL checked.
build_plan: Stack: single Next.js page on Vercel/Netlify (Netlify free tier: 125k function invocations/mo, confirmed) + one serverless route holding the Parallel key server-side (never in the browser — key is header-auth, CORS unconfirmed). Steps: (1) /api/check fetches the URL, strips to text with Readability, and sends it to a cheap LLM with one job: extract 8-20 atomic, checkable claims about software (versions, prices, model names, limits, flags, "X is the latest") and discard opinions; (2) send all claims as named `noul` questions in ONE Parallel Decisions request with the page's topic as `state` — get back a probability per claim plus a top-level citations array; (3) bucket p>0.75 still true, p<0.35 out of date, else unverifiable; Still True score = share of checked claims still true; (4) render the result page: claims listed with verdicts and the source link, plus an OG image (@vercel/og) of the card — title, big score, 3 reddest claims, date — so the result link previews in a post; (5) "Watch this page" = store URL in a KV store, a daily cron re-checks ~200 watched URLs and shows a sparkline of the score over time plus "2 claims rotted this week"; (6) seed a public "Rot Board" of 30 well-known docs/tutorial pages the builder checks weekly, so first-time visitors land on something alive. Cut: accounts, email, PDF, bulk crawling, auto-fixing the text, any claim that isn't about software.
launch_post:
Paste a URL. Expiry reads your post, pulls out every factual claim about software, and checks each one against the live web.

You get a Still True score out of 100 and a list of what rotted — model names, pricing, flags, "the latest version is".

My own 2024 tutorial scored 41. Free, open source.
reasoning:
Expiry beat the others on three counts. First, it is the only candidate where a thing released yesterday — Parallel's Decisions API, $0.001 for up to 100 typed, web-grounded, cited questions — turns a previously fiddly pipeline into one HTTP call, which is exactly the LlamaCoder pattern in the taste file: ride a new capability while it is fresh. Second, the input is personal in the way roomGPT and restorePhotos are personal: it is YOUR post, YOUR README, and the result is a number about your own work, which is why a self-own launch post ("my own tutorial scored 41") works. Third, the sharpen rounds gave it a reason to return that none of the toys had — a watched page whose score drops over weeks, and a public Rot Board that changes on its own. The forecasting candidates all died on prior art (Oracle Markets, OddsShopper), the LFM3 ones on unverified in-browser deployment, and the skill ones on being repeats of Shelf and Skillscope. Expiry touches the same bookmark neighbourhood as Shelf/Skillscope (agent skills) but the audience and workflow are different: it is for anyone who writes about software, the input is any URL, and the output is a time-series freshness score, not a static X-ray of one file. No overlap with tonight's venture (Payeeproof, vendor bank-change verification for public-sector finance staff): different buyer, different problem, nothing shared but the word "evidence". could_grow is true — the paid shape is a weekly crawl of a company's docs site and changelog that files tickets for rotted pages, which devrel teams already do badly by hand — but that is a separate venture conversation, not this weekend.

Runner-up (Venture, 7.6): Payeeproof won because it was the only candidate where I could find, in public documents, the buyer, the failure, the dollar amount and the exact missing artefact in the same place. State auditors are writing the sales pitch: Florida AG reports name districts with no record of independent verification for 54 address changes and 8 of 10 bank changes, and recommend documenting "who requested, verified, authorized and entered" each change — which is literally the product's output PDF. Losses are concrete and recent (Mansfield $54k, Texarkana ~$2M with $204,890 unrecovered, Sudbury $12.8k in payroll diversion, Mobile $14.7M reported). Nacha Phase 2 on 22 June 2026 made documented risk-based processes an obligation for every non-consumer ACH originator, and TASB's risk pool warns that failing to independently authenticate payment instructions can jeopardise cyber coverage — so there are three separate people who can force the purchase. It does not repeat anything in the library: Receipts files evidence of payer-portal submissions for medical billers, Holdroom supervises live AI phone calls for ops teams, and Mandate approves outbound insurance-agency messages. Payeeproof's buyer is a public-sector business manager and its workflow is inbound payee-change verification, a different event entirely; the AI callback is one step inside it rather than the product. It also fits the builder: a forwarding inbox, a hosted voice agent, a typed-output model and a PDF generator is a two-to-four-week v1 in TypeScript, and the ERP write-back later is exactly UiPath work. What keeps it off an 8: I could not find a single published price paid by a small district for a tool like this, and I could not confirm the AI callback connects at a useful rate against small-vendor phone lines. Those are the two things to test this week, and both are cheap.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Skill-diet-as-a-service / agent context budget monitor for platform teams (from @nicopreme) — dropped at generate: too close to past ideas Shelf and Skillscope, same buyer (agent builders), and the free OSS skill already does it. 2. Agent tool-call approval gateway for non-engineering teams (from @digitalocean Action Gateway) — dropped at generate: this is Holdroom in the library, and DigitalOcean/NVIDIA are now shipping it natively. 3. On-device multimodal inspection agent for field trades using LFM3-VL (from @liquidai) — dropped at screen: real buyer (insurance/utility field inspectors) but needs hardware, long sales cycle, and 3+ months before a first sale; wrong fit for evenings and weekends. 4. Web-grounded lead/customer record refresher built on the Parallel Decisions API (from @p0) — dropped at screen: Fiber AI, Clay and a dozen enrichment vendors already sell exactly this to exactly this buyer; crowded and the API is a commodity anyone can call. 5. Supplier master-data hygiene agent for procurement (stale banking, duplicates, dead vendors) — finalist, but merged into the pick: data-quality framing has no urgency and competes with Ivalua/apexanalytix; the change-request moment is where the money and the deadline are. 6. HTS/tariff reclassification watcher for small importers — dropped at screen: 2026 is thick with trade-compliance vendors (Gaia Dynamics, Quickcode, bitedata) chasing the same tariff churn, and the builder has no customs domain access. 7. Carrier appetite-change tracker for independent insurance agencies — dropped at screen: adjacent to the library's Mandate (same buyer), and First Connect and the MGA platforms already aggregate appetite. 8. Grant-condition change monitor for nonprofit grants managers — dropped at screen: real latent pain, but Instrumentl and Thompson Grants occupy the space, budgets are thin and the compliance event is annual, not weekly. 9. Periodic KYB/CDD refresh desk for credit unions and small banks — dropped at screen: heavily funded incumbents (Alloy, Sardine, Abrigo across 2,500 institutions) and a 9-month regulated sales cycle. 10. Payeeproof: payee-change verification and evidence desk for small public finance offices — PICK. Named buyer, recurring weekly event, a June 2026 compliance deadline, published audit findings naming the exact missing artefact, and the incumbents are all enterprise-priced portals.

PROJECT
1. Expiry — URL in, per-claim freshness card with a Still True score + weekly re-check. PICK: new API makes it newly cheap, personal (your own post), output is a number people post, weekly reason to return.
2. Oracle — paste any "will X happen" question, get a web-grounded probability card. Finalist, lost: Oracle Markets, OddsShopper and OrcaLayer already publish AI-vs-market probability dashboards with Brier scores; crowded and the output is a number with no personal stake.
3. Drift Board — AI's probability vs Polymarket odds, biggest disagreements daily. Dropped at screen: github shows many LLM-vs-market tools (homerun, polymarket-agents, OctagonAI kalshi bot) and oraclemarkets.io does exactly this.
4. SkillSlim web — paste a SKILL.md, see what a diet would cut. Dropped: thin clone of nicopreme's skill-diet, and too close to past ideas Shelf/Skillscope.
5. Lens — LFM3-VL-2B running on-device, webcam in, spatial description out. Finalist, lost: browser deployment unconfirmed (ONNX export exists but no verified in-browser runtime), so buildability risk over a weekend is real.
6. EarCheck — LFM3-Audio-2B turns a voice memo into typed decisions. Dropped at screen: needs local GPU/laptop setup, not a link anyone can click.
7. Hetzner Bill — paste your AWS bill, see the bare-metal equivalent (from @SimonHoiberg's $8k→$300). Dropped: needs bill parsing plus made-up equivalence; a calculator, nothing to share twice.
8. Gate — paste an agent's tool-call log, get an allow/deny/ask policy card (from the DigitalOcean Action Gateway post). Dropped: audience too small, output not shareable, and overlaps past idea Proofline/Holdroom territory.
9. RWE Cards — turn the RWE-Bench physical-engineering tasks into a browsable card wall. Dropped at screen: dataset contents and licence unverified, and it is a gallery with no personal input.
10. Mode — a browsable wall of the focus "modes" people build for AI docks (from @trq212). Dropped: no public dataset exists, would have to be invented.
research_notes:
Venture: Reading pot (3 of 3): Parallel Decisions API (confirmed $0.001/request, web-grounded typed decisions, explicitly pitched at "refresh stale banking records" — which seeded the payee-data angle), DigitalOcean Action Gateway (confirmed it is a shipped allow/deny/ask tool-policy layer, which killed candidate 2 as a repeat of Holdroom against a now-native feature), Liquid LFM3 / d1 decision models (typed outputs and calibrated probabilities on 2B open-weight models, fine-tunable on one GPU — the cheap classifier layer in the build plan). I also spent one extra summary on skill-diet, which confirmed candidate 1 was a solved OSS problem.

Screening pot (6 of 6): one search each on eligibility-rule monitoring, supplier master data, KYB refresh, carrier appetite, grant compliance and HTS/tariff. Four died here on crowding or sales-cycle length. The supplier master-data search was the one that paid off — it surfaced "stale banking details" and vendor-change fraud as the live, named pain inside an otherwise boring data-quality category, which redirected the whole night.

Deep research pot (12 of 12): mapped the competitive floor and ceiling (Trustpair/PaymentWorks/Eftsure/apexanalytix all quote-only and enterprise-shaped; nsKnox Essentials at $800/mo with an AI Agent Caller; CallbackProof at $99–$199/mo for bookkeeping firms; BankChangeGuard at $99/mo for QBO), established the regulatory clock (Nacha Phase 1 20 Mar 2026, Phase 2 22 Jun 2026, risk-based and documentation-shaped with no prescribed product), gathered the loss and audit evidence (Mansfield $54k, Texarkana ~$2M / $204,890 unrecovered, Sudbury $12,825 payroll, Broward 40 unreviewed change requests, Mobile $14.7M reported, Florida AG findings naming Orange/Charlotte/Okeechobee, Washington SAO on Mercer Island, a Florida report citing $359,566 misdirected), checked the insurance angle (2026 coverage disputes turning on documented callbacks; TASB RMF tying independent authentication to coverage), sized the buyer universe (~13,300 districts, ~19,500 municipalities), and priced the callback technology (Vapi/Retell/Bland/ElevenLabs ~$0.07–$0.31/min, plus all-party-consent recording constraints). Two searches returned nothing usable (Reddit AP complaints, nonprofit finance directors) — that absence is why market_pull is capped at 7: I have audit evidence, not purchase evidence.

Sharpening pot (2 of 5): one call confirmed Florida's vendor-change findings are a recurring statutory audit objective rather than a one-off, and one confirmed employee direct-deposit changes are a separately audited, separately lossy failure mode worth folding into the same desk. Three sharpening calls unspent because the two changes both survived first contact and further calls were unlikely to move a score I could defend; the remaining unknowns (district price points, callback connect rates) need primary contact, not search — which is what the validation test does this week.
Sharpening (7 to 7.6): Round 1 — weakest criterion: gap (6 before). The original candidate was a generic "AI vendor bank-change verification for mid-market finance teams." Research found that space is genuinely contested at the low end: nsKnox publishes an SMB tier at $800/mo and markets an AI Agent Caller that places, records and summarises verification calls; CallbackProof sells a $99–$199/mo hash-chained callback log; BankChangeGuard sells a $99/mo QuickBooks workflow. So I changed the idea: move the buyer from the generic mid-market controller to the small public finance office (K-12 district business manager, town comptroller), where the forcing function is not ROI but a recurring statutory operational audit. Evidence that held: Florida AG audits repeatedly cite exactly this control across multiple districts (Orange, Charlotte, Okeechobee, plus a report citing $359,566 misdirected and recommending a vendor-change log); Florida statute requires district operational audits at least every three years; Washington SAO made the same finding against the City of Mercer Island; TASB RMF ties independent authentication to coverage. None of the three cheap incumbents targets or integrates with this buyer — CallbackProof sells to bookkeeping firms, BankChangeGuard to QuickBooks companies, nsKnox to corporate treasury — and the enterprise players (PaymentWorks, Trustpair, Eftsure) sell portal onboarding at quote-only prices. gap 6 → 8; pain 7 → 8 on the named losses and findings.

Round 2 — weakest remaining: timing (7 before) and market_pull (7). Change to the idea: widen the change types from vendor bank details to all payee-detail changes including employee direct deposit, and anchor the evidence pack's wording on the Nacha Phase 2 obligation. Evidence found: Nacha Phase 2 bound every remaining non-consumer originator on 22 June 2026 to documented, annually reviewed, risk-based fraud processes — a documentation mandate, not a product mandate, which is precisely what a cheap evidence tool satisfies; and payroll diversion is an independently documented, separately audited failure (Sudbury Public Schools, $12,825 across two payrolls, changes approved with no independent confirmation; Minnesota OSA and NY Comptroller both publish direct-deposit verification guidance). That roughly doubles the number of change events per customer per month and gives the payroll director as a second internal champion. timing 7 → 8. market_pull stayed at 7: I confirmed the role, the obligation and the audit pressure, but found no published price any district actually pays for this category, so I will not score the budget line above 7 on inference. First score (average before sharpening) 7.0 → 7.6.

Project: Reading pot (3/3): summarised the Parallel Decisions API launch (confirmed $0.001/request, 100 questions per request, 5,000 free requests, 600 rpm, 200ms–1s), the LFM3 release (six ~2B models, LFM Open License v1.0, on HF with ONNX for VL, but NO confirmed in-browser deployment — this killed two candidates), and Decisions request/auth shape (x-api-key header, CORS unconfirmed → must use a serverless proxy, which set the build plan). Screening pot (5/5): searched prior art for pasted-claim fact-checkers, AI-probability forecast apps, landing-page claim scorers, Polymarket/Kalshi public APIs, and LLM-vs-market dashboards — the forecasting candidates died here (oraclemarkets.io, OddsShopper AI-vs-market scoreboard, several GitHub LLM-vs-odds tools). Deep research (8/8): confirmed no URL→README/claim freshness checker exists (closest: BCGen `skill-auditing` and bootgs `freshness-auditor` agent skills, SERP Delta with zero stars, HowToAI's paste-text hallucination checker); confirmed Parallel ToS permit public apps with per-visitor results but bar republishing stored output (so the Rot Board must be the builder's own small curated set, not a bulk dataset); confirmed Decisions supports choice/score types and returns response-level (not per-answer) citations — this changed the UI design so citations are shown as "what's true now" context, never as per-claim proof; confirmed Netlify free tier (125k invocations) covers launch. Sharpening pot (4/4): checked docs-rot leaderboards (DocsAlot, 215 sites, stale since June 2026), freshness/"still true" badges (only timestamp badges exist — Shields.io, cardd.cc), GitHub-Action docs-freshness tools (DocGuard checks commits-since-review, not web truth), and developer complaints about stale guidance. The weekly-watch and score-card changes survived; nothing well known does either.
Sharpening (7.8 to 8.4): Round 1 — weak criterion: usefulness (7, a one-time "check my old post" toy). Change: added "Watch weekly" — save a URL, a daily cron re-checks it, and the page shows the Still True score over time plus "2 claims rotted this week"; plus a public Rot Board of ~30 well-known docs pages re-scored weekly so the site itself changes. Research: checked for prior art on docs-rot leaderboards and freshness badges — DocsAlot ranks 215 docs sites but site-level and last updated June 2026; Shields.io/cardd.cc badges only show a timestamp, never whether claims hold; no page-level weekly rot index found. Cost check: at $0.001 per Decisions request with 100 questions bundled, 200 watched pages re-checked daily is ~$6/month, inside the free $5 allowance at weekly cadence. Usefulness 7 → 8.
Round 2 — weak criterion: shareability (7, a list of verdicts is not a post). Change: the primary output became a card with one number on it (Still True 41/100) rendered as an OG image so the result link previews in a tweet, with the 3 reddest claims on it. Research: confirmed no existing tool produces a "% still true" card (closest are age-only freshness badges), so the number is novel and the self-own format ("my own tutorial scored 41") is the hook. Shareability 7 → 8. Wow stayed 8, not 9: the result is surprising but it is a verdict list, not something people screen-record.
prototype_summary: Expiry is a freshness checker that scans a URL, scores how much of the post is still true, flags out-of-date claims with what's true now, and offers a shareable score card, weekly watch sparkline, and a Rot Board of decaying docs.
